title: 📘 UNIT 5: PEOPLES AND STATES OF AFRICA TO 1500
notes:
Africa → one of the major cradles of humanity and an important center of ancient and medieval cultures and civilizations.

Major historical themes → linguistic diversity + state formation + trade + Islam + cultural interaction + agriculture + maritime commerce.

Important African centers and states → Mamluk Egypt + Aksum + Ghana + Mali + Songhai + Kanem-Bornu + Hausa city-states + Swahili city-states + Great Zimbabwe + Khoi-Khoi and San.

📌 Trade was one of the strongest forces connecting different regions of Africa and encouraging the growth of states.

title: 5.1 🗣️ Ancient and Medieval African States
notes:
Africa contains about 1,000–2,000 languages, making it one of the world's most linguistically diverse continents.

At least 75 African languages have one million or more speakers.

Nigeria → around 500 languages.

Major African language families/phyla:
• Niger-Congo.
• Afro-Asiatic.
• Nilo-Saharan.
• Khoisan.

📌 These language groups reflect the long history of migration, settlement and interaction among African peoples.

title: 5.1.1 🔤 African Languages: Classification and Distribution
notes:
🟢 Niger-Congo → largest African language family; mainly found in western, central and southeastern Africa.

Bantu languages → major branch of Niger-Congo, especially widespread toward southern Africa.
Examples → Swahili, Yoruba, Kirundi, Lingala, Sesotho and Shona.

🟡 Afro-Asiatic → around 200–300 languages.
Major examples → Arabic, Somali, Amharic, Afan Oromo, Berber and Hausa.
Arabic → especially widespread in North Africa.

🔵 Nilo-Saharan → around 80 languages, distributed mainly across parts of central, eastern and northeastern Africa.
Examples → Lugbara, Zarma and Dholuo.

🟠 Khoisan → around 40–70 languages, mainly concentrated in southern Africa, especially Botswana, Namibia, South Africa and Angola.
Examples → Hadza and Naro.

📌 Swahili → Bantu language strongly influenced by Arabic through centuries of trade and became an important lingua franca of East Africa.

title: 5.2 🌍 North Africa
notes:
North Africa → major historical region linking Africa with the Mediterranean, Middle East and Europe.

Important developments → Mamluk rule in Egypt + Islamic expansion + Almoravid movement + Almohad movement.

Major political and economic connections → Red Sea trade + Mediterranean trade + Trans-Saharan trade.

title: 5.2.1 🏛️ Mamluk Egypt
notes:
Mamluks → military aristocracy that ruled Egypt from about 1250 to 1517.

Mamluk → Arabic word meaning 'owned' or 'slave'.

Originally → Turkish slaves brought to Egypt and trained as soldiers.

Before 1250 → Egypt was ruled by the Ayyubid Sultanate.

👑 Al-Malik al-Salih → Ayyubid sultan who organized a Mamluk mercenary regiment.

Rise of Mamluks → Ayyubid family rivalry + dependence on military slaves + Crusader invasion + Mongol threat.

1250 → Mamluks seized political power in Egypt.

⚔️ Crusades → Mamluks defeated the Crusaders and captured Louis IX of France.

⚔️ Mongols → Mamluks also defeated Mongol forces, increasing their prestige as defenders of Islam.

title: 5.2.1.1 💰 Mamluk Economic and Cultural Achievements
notes:
Mamluk Egypt experienced economic prosperity and cultural development.

Major achievements →
• Architecture.
• Craftsmanship.
• Scholarship.
• Military strategy literature.
• Strong military organization.

🏇 Polo → popular among Mamluks because of its similarity to military activities.

💰 Economic prosperity came from:
• Trans-Saharan trade.
• Gold brought from West Africa.
• Pilgrimage traffic to Mecca.
• Spice trade connecting the Far East, Red Sea and Mediterranean.

1275 → Mamluks controlled Nubia and promoted its Islamization.

📌 Cairo → important commercial center because West African gold and other goods passed through it.

title: 5.2.1.2 📉 End of Mamluk Rule
notes:
Main external pressure → Ottoman Turks.

1516 → Ottoman Turks took control of Egypt.

1517 → Mamluk political rule officially ended.

Major Ottoman motivation → competition with Portugal over control of the Red Sea and Indian Ocean trade.

1517–1805 → Mamluks continued to exercise influence in Egypt under Ottoman suzerainty.

📌 Mohammed Ali → established a new ruling dynasty in Egypt in 1805.

title: 5.3 ☪️ Spread of Islam to North Africa
notes:
Maghreb → western half of North Africa, including present-day Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia and Mauritania.

Two major Islamic movements played important roles in the spread and consolidation of Islam in the Maghreb:
• Almoravids.
• Almohads.

title: 5.3.1 🏜️ Almoravid Movement
notes:
Almoravids → Muslim Berber movement that emerged among nomadic peoples of the Maghreb in the 11th century.

Origin → Lamtuna, a nomadic Muslim Berber tribe.

👤 Ibn Yasin → important early religious leader.
👤 Emir Yahya → major political leader.
👤 Abu Bakar → succeeded Ibn Yasin after his death.

Main objective → return to the strict and pure practice of Islam.

1042–1053 → formative period of the movement.

1062 → Marrakesh became the capital.

1080s → Almoravids controlled Morocco and western Algeria.

1110 → Saragossa fell to the Almoravids.

Political structure → strongly tribal, with the Lamtuna exercising major influence.

📌 Almoravids contributed to the spread of Islam and development of Maghreb culture.

title: 5.3.2 🕌 Almohad Movement
notes:
Almohads → religious and political reform movement that replaced Almoravid power in the 12th century.

Origin → Masmuda Berbers of the Atlas Mountains.

👤 Ibn Tumart → founder of the Almohad religious reform movement.

Main ideas → strict religious reform + Quran as the main source of Islamic life + rejection of practices considered contrary to Islam.

1130 → Ibn Tumart died.

👤 Abdul Mumin → succeeded Ibn Tumart and became the main political founder of the Almohad Empire.

Almohads → defeated and replaced the Almoravids and expanded across the Maghreb and into Spain.

📉 Decline → Muslim internal divisions + Christian attacks in Spain + internal division and civil war.

1269 → Almohad rule in North Africa ended.

title: 5.4 🏺 States in West Africa
notes:
West Africa → region stretching roughly from Lake Chad in the east toward the Senegal, Gambia and Niger Rivers in the west.

Also called → Western Sudan or Bilad al-Sudan.

Major states →
• Ghana.
• Mali.
• Songhai.
• Kanem-Bornu.
• Hausa city-states.

Economic foundation → Trans-Saharan trade + agriculture + livestock + crafts.

Major trade goods → gold + salt + slaves + cloth + kola nuts + animal products.

📌 Trade routes connected West Africa with North Africa and the Mediterranean world.

title: 5.4.1 🟡 Empire of Ghana
notes:
Ghana → oldest known kingdom in Western Sudan.

👥 Founded by → Soninke people.
📅 Foundation → around the 4th century.
📈 Height → around 1000 A.D.

📍 Political center → Kumbi Saleh.
📍 Economic center → Awadaghust.

Economic foundation → Trans-Saharan trade.

Ghana's location → between North African markets and the forest regions of West Africa.

Major advantage → acted as middlemen between northern traders and southern producers.

💰 Trade income → financed a strong central government and army.

⚔️ Military power → helped Ghana conquer neighboring peoples.

🔨 Ironworking → skilled Ghanaian craftsmen gave the kingdom military and economic advantages.

Territory → extended across much of present-day Mali and Mauritania.

📉 Decline → Almoravid attacks.

1054 → Almoravids captured Awadaghust.
1076 → Almoravids captured Kumbi Saleh.

📌 Loss of the economic and political centers contributed to the end of Ghana's power.

title: 5.4.2 🟢 Empire of Mali
notes:
Mali → emerged after the decline of Ghana.

👥 People → Mandinka.

👤 Sundiata → founder and major early ruler of Mali.
📅 Reign → approximately 1230–1255.

1235 → Sundiata defeated his enemies, gained control of important gold routes and established Mali's power.

Major gold fields → Wangara and Bambuk.

📈 Golden age → reign of Mansa Musa (1312–1337).

👑 Mansa Musa → most famous ruler of Mali and an important Muslim ruler.

1324 → Mansa Musa made a famous pilgrimage to Mecca with a large caravan and enormous quantities of gold.

His pilgrimage → demonstrated Mali's wealth and strengthened its connections with the wider Muslim world.

Major achievements → development of cities + mosques + Islamic scholarship + expansion of trade.

📉 Decline → weak rulers + difficulty controlling the large empire + internal struggles + attacks from Mossi, Tuareg and Songhai.

Mali continued until about 1550, but later rulers exercised mainly nominal authority.

title: 5.4.3 🔵 Empire of Songhai
notes:
Songhai → rose as Mali weakened during the 15th century.

📍 Capital → Gao.

📈 Major expansion → under Sunni Ali (1464–1492).

👑 Sunni Ali → created the largest state that had existed in West Africa at that time.

Major achievements →
• Controlled important trade routes.
• Captured Timbuktu.
• Expanded territory.
• Strengthened political power.

🙏 Religion → Sunni Ali followed indigenous religion rather than Islam.

👑 Askia Muhammad → established a Muslim dynasty after Sunni Ali's death.

Major reforms →
• Expanded territory.
• Organized bureaucracy.
• Separate departments for agriculture, military and treasury.
• Strengthened Islamic education.
• Built mosques and schools.

🕋 Askia Muhammad → made pilgrimage to Mecca and strengthened relations with the Muslim world.

📚 Timbuktu and Gao → important centers of Islamic scholarship and intellectual life.

title: 5.4.3.1 📉 Decline of Songhai
notes:
After Askia Muhammad → succession disputes weakened political stability.

1549 → Askia Daud became emperor and brought relative peace.

1582 → Askia Daud died; succession conflicts increased.

Result → civil war and political weakness.

👑 Ahmed al-Mansur → Sultan of Morocco who sent an army south to control Songhai's gold and salt resources.

1591 → Moroccan forces defeated Songhai using gunpowder weapons.

📌 Result → Songhai Empire disintegrated and Moroccan control was established over parts of the Niger region.

The Moroccan rulers could not effectively maintain control over the enormous territory across the Sahara.

title: 5.4.4 🏜️ Empire of Kanem-Bornu
notes:
Kanem-Bornu → long-lasting African trading empire centered around Lake Chad.

📅 Period → approximately 9th–19th centuries.

👥 People → Kanuri.
👑 Dynasty → Saifuwa.
📍 Early capital → Njimi.

Territory included areas of present-day:
• Chad.
• Cameroon.
• Nigeria.
• Niger.
• Libya.

Economic foundation → Trans-Saharan trade.

Geographical position → connected Nubia, Egypt, North Africa and western/southern regions.

11th century → Islam became the accepted religion.

Expansion → reached toward the Niger River, Wadai and Fezzan.

14th century → wars with the Bulala forced the ruling family westward into Bornu.

👑 Ali Ghaji → established a new capital at Ngazargamu.

👑 Mai Idris Alooma → strengthened Kanem-Bornu in the 16th century and acquired firearms from Turks in North Africa.

📉 Decline → Fulani infiltration + Islamic revivalist movements + rise of neighboring states.

1846 → Wadai absorbed Kanem, marking the end of one of West Africa's longest-lasting empires.

title: 5.4.5 🏙️ Hausa City-States
notes:
Hausa city-states → independent urban states established mainly in present-day northern Nigeria.

Major city-states → Daura + Gobir + Rano + Katsina + Zazzau/Zaria + Kano + Biram.

📅 Early emergence → around 1000 A.D.

Political form → city-state = independent political unit centered on a city.

Economic foundation → Trans-Saharan trade + agriculture.

Major trade goods → leather + gold + cloth + salt + kola nuts + animal hides + slaves.

Hausa cities → served as southern terminals of Trans-Saharan caravan routes.

By 1200 → Hausa city-states had Muslim rulers.

Specialization:
• Kano and Katsina → trade and crafts.
• Daura → ironworking.
• Zaria → major supplier of slaves.

📈 Kano → largest and most prosperous Hausa city by the 1500s and an important Islamic cultural center.

Political relationship → cities remained independent, sometimes cooperating and often competing with one another.

1804 → Usman dan Fodio began a jihad.
1815 → Hausa city-states were incorporated into the Sokoto Caliphate.

title: 5.4.6 ☪️ Spread of Islam in West Africa
notes:
Islam reached West Africa by about the 8th century but spread gradually.

Main agents → Muslim merchants + North African traders + scholars + rulers.

📌 Trade was the major channel through which Islam spread.

Important Trans-Saharan routes →
• Sijilmasa → Awdaghust.
• Ghadames → Gao.

Trade centers gradually became centers of Islamic learning and culture.

👑 Tekrur → accepted Islam as early as 850 A.D. under the Dya'ogo dynasty.

11th century → Islam entered Ghana.

Mali → rulers increasingly accepted Islam, especially during the 14th century.

👑 Mansa Musa → devout Muslim; pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324; promoted mosques and Islamic culture.

8th–14th centuries → Islam became firmly established in many regions associated with Ghana, Mali, Songhai and Hausa city-states.

title: 5.5 🌊 Central and Eastern Africa
notes:
Eastern African coast → stretched from Somalia in the north to Mozambique in the south.

Major historical features → maritime trade + Indian Ocean connections + Islam + urban city-states + cultural interaction.

Swahili peoples → developed maritime trading societies along the coast.

Important external connections → Arabia + Persia + India + China + Mediterranean world.

📌 Indian Ocean monsoon winds → made regular sailing voyages along the East African coast possible.

title: 5.5.1 🚢 East African Coast, Islam and Trade
notes:
📜 Periplus of the Erythraean Sea → 1st-century A.D. Greek merchant guide describing Red Sea and East African coastal trade.

Major trade goods → ivory + rhinoceros horn + tortoise shell + palm oil.

🌍 Zanj/Swahili Coast → coastal region from Somalia to Mozambique.

Original inhabitants → mainly Bantu-speaking Africans who migrated toward the coast from the interior.

Important settlements → Shungwaya + Malindi + Gedi + Mombasa.

By the late medieval period → at least 37 substantial Swahili trading towns existed.

Political organization → independent city-states rather than one unified empire.

Arab and Persian immigrants → became important in ruling and commercial classes.

8th century → Muslim Arab traders began permanent settlement.

12th century → Persian settlers known as Shirazi arrived.

Religion → majority of Swahili people became Sunni Muslims.

Swahili language → Bantu language with strong Arabic influence and additional Persian, Portuguese and German loanwords.

title: 5.5.2 🏝️ Major Swahili City-States
notes:
Major Swahili trading centers → Kilwa + Mombasa + Malindi + Mogadishu + Gedi and others.

📈 Peak period → approximately 11th–15th centuries.

🏛️ Political structure → independent Muslim sultanates sharing Swahili language and Islamic religion.

🚢 Trade → pottery + silk + glassware + ivory + gold + other goods.

⭐ Kilwa → one of the most important southern Swahili city-states.

Kilwa maintained an outpost at Sofala → important for trade with the gold-rich Great Zimbabwe region.

🇨🇳 Zheng He → Chinese admiral whose expeditions reached Mombasa, Malindi and Mogadishu.

Chinese expeditions → diplomatic and commercial contacts rather than permanent colonization.

1497–1498 → Vasco da Gama sailed around the Cape of Good Hope and reached the East African coast.

Portuguese objective → control Indian Ocean commerce.

📉 Portuguese intervention → reduced trade and contributed to the decline of several Swahili city-states.

title: 5.6 🗿 Southern Africa
notes:
Southern Africa → home to Bantu-speaking peoples, Khoi-Khoi and San.

Major historical development → growth of organized societies, agriculture, pastoralism, mining, trade and state formation.

Important topics → Great Zimbabwe + Khoi-Khoi + San.

📌 Southern African societies developed distinctive political, economic and cultural systems before European colonization.

title: 5.6.1 🏛️ Great Zimbabwe
notes:
Great Zimbabwe → powerful inland state and major center of early Shona civilization.

Zimbabwe → Bantu-based word meaning 'stone house'.

👥 Builders → Bantu-speaking peoples, particularly the Shona.

📅 Settlement and development → approximately 900–1500 A.D.

Economic activities → cattle keeping + agriculture + ironworking + mining + long-distance trade + crafts.

Early settlers → raised cattle and built stone enclosures.

📈 Height → around 1300 A.D.

💰 Gold → important economic resource.

🚢 Trade connections → Sofala and Kilwa on the East African coast.

🌍 International evidence → Indian beads and Chinese porcelain show connections with the wider Indian Ocean trading network.

Skilled crafts → jewelry making + cotton weaving.

🏛️ Architecture → massive stone walls + palaces + cone-shaped towers.

📌 Great Zimbabwe demonstrates advanced stone construction and organized economic activity in medieval southern Africa.

title: 5.6.1.1 📉 Decline of Great Zimbabwe
notes:
Great Zimbabwe began to decline around 1500 A.D.

Possible causes →
• Overpopulation.
• Environmental exploitation.
• Civil war.
• Declining trade.
• Shifting trade routes.

Portuguese traders → increasingly moved inland searching for gold sources.

📌 After Great Zimbabwe declined, its political and economic position was taken over by successor states including Mutapa.

title: 5.6.2 🐄 Khoi-Khoi
notes:
Khoi-Khoi → southern African people whose economy became mainly pastoral.

Originally → practiced hunting before gradually adopting cattle herding.

📅 From about 1300 → expanded from the region of present-day Botswana toward southern Africa.

By the 15th century → well established in southern Africa.

Economic base → cattle pastoralism.

⚔️ Later pressure → Dutch settlers and Bantu-speaking peoples.

📌 Their territory became increasingly restricted, forcing many communities into less favorable areas, including parts of the Kalahari region.

title: 5.6.3 🏹 San
notes:
San → one of the long-established peoples of Southern Africa.

Traditional economy → hunting and gathering.

Social organization → small bands of roughly ten families.

👩 Women → gathered wild plants and fruits.
👨 Men → hunted animals.

Weapons → light bows and poison-tipped arrows.

Housing → caves or simple thatched shelters.

Clothing → skin aprons and sandals.

📌 San communities depended heavily on the natural environment and maintained a mobile hunter-gatherer way of life.

title: 5.7 🔄 Relationships and Exchanges among Different Regions of Africa
notes:
Before European exploration of the 15th–16th centuries → different African regions were connected through extensive internal and international trade networks.

Major connecting forces →
• Trans-Saharan trade.
• Red Sea trade.
• Indian Ocean trade.
• River and overland routes.
• Migration.
• Religious interaction.

Egyptian expeditions → connected North-East Africa with Punt.

Swahili Coast → connected East Africa with Arabia, Persia, India and China.

Sahara → connected North Africa with West Africa.

📌 Trade did more than exchange goods; it also transmitted languages, religions, technologies, ideas and cultural practices.

title: 5.7.1 🐪 Trans-Saharan Caravan Trade
notes:
Trans-Saharan trade → long-distance commercial network connecting North Africa with West Africa across the Sahara.

📅 Regular trade → developed by about the 4th century.

📈 Peak period → especially 14th–16th centuries during the height of Mali and Songhai.

Major routes →
• North–South.
• West–East.
• Southern routes.

🐪 Camel → most important pack animal for northern and western routes because it could survive desert conditions.

Southern routes → also used donkeys, human porters and canoes.

Important market centers → Fez + Marrakesh + Sijilmasa + Wadan + Awdaghust + Takrur + Taghaza + Djenné + Timbuktu + Tripoli + Ghadames + Katsina + Kano + Wadai and others.

Major gold fields → Wangara + Bambuk + Bure + Lobi-Pourra.

title: 5.7.2 🧂 Gold, Salt and Other Trade Commodities
notes:
Three essential commodities during the major period of Trans-Saharan trade →

🧂 Salt → abundant in North Africa.

🟡 Gold → abundant in West Africa.

👥 Slaves → major trade commodity across the network.

Other important goods → cloth + foodstuffs + perfumes + kola nuts + animal hides.

📍 Taghaza → important salt-producing area.
📍 Timbuktu → major commercial and intellectual center.
📍 Djenné and Niani → important markets connecting northern goods with forest products.

Forest exports → gold + kola nuts + animal hides and other products.

📌 Trade created economic interdependence between different African regions and encouraged the growth of powerful states.

notes:

Shona/Bantu-speaking peoples.

Height → around 1300 A.D.

Economy → cattle + agriculture + gold + trade.

Architecture → massive stone walls and structures.

Trade → Kilwa + Sofala + Indian Ocean network.

Decline → environmental pressure + civil war + declining/shifting trade.

🐄 KHOI-KHOI

Economy → pastoralism and cattle herding.

Originally → hunting before adopting pastoralism.

Organization → small family bands.

Women → gathering.

Men → hunting.

Weapons → bows and poison-tipped arrows.

🐪 TRANS-SAHARAN TRADE

North Africa ↔ West Africa.

Main goods → salt + gold + slaves.

Camel → key transport animal.

Major centers → Timbuktu + Djenné + Gao + Fez + Marrakesh + Kano + Katsina.

🧠 EXAM CONNECTION:

Language diversity → 4 major African language families.

Mamluks → Egypt + military power + Crusades + Mongols.

Almoravids → Maghreb + strict Islam.

Almohads → religious reform + replacement of Almoravids.

Ghana → gold + salt trade + Soninke.

Mali → Sundiata + Mansa Musa + gold.

Songhai → Sunni Ali + Askia Muhammad + Timbuktu.

Kanem-Bornu → Lake Chad + Saifuwa + Islam.

Hausa → city-states + trade + agriculture.

Swahili → Indian Ocean trade + Islam + maritime city-states.

Great Zimbabwe → Shona + stone architecture + gold trade.

Khoi-Khoi → pastoralism.
San → hunting and gathering.

📌 KEY DATES:
4th century → regular Trans-Saharan trade developed.

c.4th century → Ghana emerged.

850 A.D. → Tekrur accepted Islam.

1000 A.D. → Hausa city-states emerged.

1054 → Almoravids captured Awadaghust.

1076 → Almoravids captured Kumbi Saleh.

1250 → Mamluks seized Egypt.

1235 → Sundiata established Mali's control over important gold routes.

1312–1337 → reign of Mansa Musa.

📌 BIG IDEA:
Trade connected Africa's regions economically and culturally. Gold, salt, slaves and other commodities supported powerful states, while trade routes also helped spread Islam, languages, technologies, ideas and cultural traditions across the continent.
